title: Constipation and a change in bowel habit in a 62-year-old woman
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 62-year-old retired shop manager in general practice with 5 to 6 months of constipation, straining, tenesmus, fatigue and small amounts of blood mixed with her stool. Her brother was recently diagnosed with bowel cancer at 48, and she has come in hoping for a faecal occult blood test. The candidate then interprets her blood tests, recognises iron deficiency anaemia, treats suspected colorectal cancer as the leading diagnosis until it is excluded, explains why a screening FOBT is the wrong test, and arranges urgent colonoscopy and safety netting.
focus: Picking up the red flags for colorectal cancer in a constipation history, and arranging urgent diagnostic colonoscopy instead of an FOBT
stem: You are an intern on your general practice rotation. Jane Doe, a 62-year-old retired shop manager, has come to the clinic because her bowel habits have changed. Your supervising GP has asked you to assess her.
tasks: Take a focused history from Ms Doe and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Ms Doe's full blood count, iron studies and biochemistry results, then ask you to give an ISBAR handover that includes your interpretation, your most likely diagnosis and differentials, your management and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Jane Doe, a 62-year-old retired shop manager. You are calm and chatty, but underneath you are worried, because your younger brother was diagnosed with bowel cancer six months ago. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I've noticed some constipation recently."

Your bowels (give only when asked):

  • It started about 5 to 6 months ago and came on gradually.
  • You used to go every day. Now you go every 3 to 4 days.
  • The stools are well formed. There is no mucus, and they are not pale, greasy or floating.
  • You have to strain. Afterwards you often feel you haven't finished (only if asked about incomplete emptying or a feeling of needing to go again).
  • You are still passing wind normally.
  • Now and then there is a small amount of blood mixed in with the poo. It is darkish red and there isn't much. You haven't thought much of it. It is mixed through the stool, not just on the toilet paper or dripping into the bowl.
  • If asked: the poo has never been black, tarry or sticky.
  • You tried Metamucil once a day for the last couple of months. It made no real difference.

Other symptoms (only if asked): you have been more tired than usual for a few months.

Say no to all of these if asked:

  • Weight loss, loss of appetite, fevers or night sweats, lumps in your neck, armpits or groin.
  • Tummy pain, cramps, bloating, or pain that eases when you open your bowels.
  • Vomiting, or a swollen tummy.
  • Diarrhoea, or swapping between diarrhoea and constipation, or urgency.
  • Pain when you open your bowels, a lump coming out of your bottom, or itching.
  • Fever with pain low on the left side of your tummy.
  • Feeling cold all the time, weight gain, dry skin or hair changes.
  • Losing control of your bowels or bladder, weakness or numbness in your legs, or numbness around your bottom.
  • Trouble passing urine, or blood in your urine.
  • Any bleeding from the vagina (you went through menopause in your early fifties).
  • Mouth ulcers, joint pains, or red, sore eyes.

Impact (only if asked): it isn't really affecting your day-to-day life.

Past medical history:

  • Haemorrhoids, removed in an operation in 2018. No problems since.
  • Osteoporosis.
  • You have never had a colonoscopy. If asked about bowel screening: "They send me those poo test kits in the mail, but I usually just ignore them."

Medications:

  • Denosumab (Prolia) injection every 6 months for your bones.
  • Metamucil once a day.
  • A multivitamin with vitamin D.
  • No pain killers such as codeine, ibuprofen or aspirin, no iron tablets, no separate calcium tablets, nothing else.

Allergies: penicillin, which gave you a rash.

Family history:

  • Your brother was diagnosed with bowel cancer six months ago, at the age of 48.
  • If asked about other relatives: you don't know of anyone else in the family with bowel cancer, polyps, womb cancer or any other cancer.
  • If asked whether your brother had genetic tests: "I'm not sure. I'd have to ask him."

Social history:

  • You smoke 10 cigarettes a day and have done for most of your adult life.
  • Alcohol: a glass of wine socially.
  • Retired shop manager.
  • You don't exercise. Your diet is balanced.
  • You live with your husband. You are independent and well supported.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: "I thought I was just getting a bit blocked up with age."
  • Concern: "With what happened to my brother, I'm worried it could be cancer."
  • Expectation: "I was hoping to get one of those bowel test kits. I usually ignore them, but after my brother I want to do one."

Question to raise once in Part 1: "Can I just do one of those poo test kits?"

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: well, comfortable, looks a little pale. Not jaundiced. Weight 68 kg, height 165 cm, BMI 25; weight unchanged from her records a year ago.
  • Observations: HR 84 regular, BP 132/80, RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C.
  • Hands: palms and palmar creases normal colour. No koilonychia, no clubbing. Nicotine staining on the right index and middle fingers.
  • Eyes and mouth: mild conjunctival pallor. No scleral icterus. No angular stomatitis or mouth ulcers.
  • Neck: no cervical or supraclavicular lymph nodes. Thyroid not enlarged.
  • Chest and heart: chest clear. Heart sounds dual, no murmurs.
  • Abdomen, inspection: not distended. No scars.
  • Abdomen, palpation: soft and non-tender in all regions. No masses, including in the left and right iliac fossae. No hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. Percussion note normal throughout; no shifting dullness.
  • Bowel sounds: present and normal.
  • Inguinal nodes: not enlarged.
  • Rectal examination (if offered with consent and a chaperone): perianal skin normal apart from healed scars from the previous haemorrhoid surgery. No external haemorrhoids, fissure, skin tags or prolapse, including on straining. Normal anal tone. No mass within reach of the finger, and the rectal wall feels smooth. Soft brown stool on the glove with streaks of dark red blood mixed through it. No melaena.
  • Proctoscopy (if offered): no internal haemorrhoids or bleeding point seen in the anal canal.
  • Lower limb neurology (if offered): normal power, reflexes and sensation, including around the saddle area.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Jane's identity and gains consent.
Uses plain language and responds with empathy to her brother's recent diagnosis and her fear of cancer.
History
Characterises the change in bowel habit:
check.d: The critical element is establishing a new, persistent change from daily to every 3–4 days over 5–6 months, with straining and incomplete emptying. Asking what she has tried earns the third sub-mark but is not needed for the critical mark.

kids.x: Onset and duration: gradual over 5 to 6 months, from daily to every 3 to 4 days.
Stool and defecation: well formed, no mucus, no pale or fatty stools; straining and a feeling of incomplete emptying (tenesmus).
What she has tried: Metamucil once a day, with no real difference.

check.x: Characterises the bleeding:

kids.x: Small amounts of darkish red blood mixed in with the stool, on and off, rather than only on the paper or dripping into the bowl.
Asks specifically about black, tarry stools (melaena) to tell a lower GI source from an upper one: none.

check.x: Screens for red flags and constitutional symptoms: weight loss, loss of appetite, fatigue (present), abdominal pain, fevers and night sweats.
check.d: Award for weight loss plus at least two of: appetite, fatigue, abdominal pain, fevers or night sweats.

check.x: Asks about bowel obstruction: vomiting, distension, colicky pain, and whether she is still passing wind (she is).

Asks questions that rule out other causes: IBS (pain eased by defecation, bloating), IBD (diarrhoea, mucus, urgency, extraintestinal symptoms), diverticular disease (left iliac fossa pain, fever), anorectal causes (painful defecation, prolapse, haemorrhoids), hypothyroidism, lymphoma (night sweats, lumps), PV bleeding, neurological causes (incontinence, leg weakness, saddle numbness) and urinary symptoms (retention, haematuria).
check.d: Award for features asked from at least four of these groups.

check.x: Takes the past medical and screening history: haemorrhoids excised in 2018 with no current problems, osteoporosis, never had a colonoscopy and has not done the bowel screening kits.

Takes a medication and allergy history, including constipating medicines: denosumab every 6 months, Metamucil, a multivitamin with vitamin D; no opioids, iron or separate calcium supplements. Penicillin allergy (rash).

Takes a family history: brother diagnosed with bowel cancer at 48, six months ago; asks about other relatives with bowel cancer, polyps or other cancers such as womb cancer (none known), and asks whether her brother had genetic or tumour testing (she is not sure).
check.d: The critical element is eliciting a first-degree relative (brother) with bowel cancer diagnosed at 48, under 55. Asking about other relatives, Lynch-type cancers and the brother's genetic or tumour testing earns full marks but is not needed for the critical mark.

check.x: Takes a social history: smokes 10 a day, social alcohol, no exercise, balanced diet, retired, lives with her husband, independent and well supported.
check.d: Award for smoking quantified plus at least two other elements.

check.x: Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations, and the impact on her life: thought it was age, worried about cancer because of her brother, hoping for an FOBT kit; no impact on daily life.
Examination
Asks for vital signs and weight, and checks the weight against previous records (normal observations, weight stable).
Looks for anaemia and spread: conjunctival pallor (mild), palmar pallor (absent), koilonychia, jaundice, and cervical, supraclavicular and inguinal lymph nodes.
Examines the abdomen: inspects for distension, palpates all regions for tenderness and masses (including both iliac fossae), feels for hepatomegaly, percusses and listens for bowel sounds.
Performs a digital rectal examination with consent and a chaperone: inspects for haemorrhoids, fissure and prolapse, palpates for a rectal mass, and notes the blood mixed with stool on the glove.
check.d: Credit offering proctoscopy as well, but it is not required.

check.x: Summarises the examination: mild pallor, normal abdomen, no mass or haemorrhoids on rectal examination, but dark red blood mixed with stool on the glove.
Interpretation
Interprets the full blood count: Hb 108 with MCV 76, low MCH and high RDW is a mild microcytic, hypochromic anaemia; the platelet count of 418 is a mild reactive rise.

Interprets the iron studies: ferritin 8, low serum iron, transferrin saturation 5% and a high transferrin confirm iron deficiency; in a postmenopausal woman this means a gastrointestinal cause, most likely blood loss, until proven otherwise.

Interprets the biochemistry: a normal TSH argues against hypothyroidism and a normal corrected calcium argues against hypercalcaemia as causes of the constipation; normal kidney and liver function, which does not exclude cancer.

Gives suspected colorectal cancer as the most likely diagnosis until proven otherwise, and justifies it: a new change in bowel habit for months at 62, blood mixed with the stool, tenesmus, fatigue with iron deficiency anaemia, a first-degree relative diagnosed under 55, and smoking.

Gives at least three differentials, each with a feature for or against (for example recurrent haemorrhoids, diverticular disease, functional constipation or IBS, hypothyroidism, an upper GI source of iron loss).
check.d: Also credit IBD, colonic polyp or anal fissure if given with a feature for or against.

check.x: Management

Explains honestly in plain words that the symptoms and blood results are concerning, that bowel cancer needs to be ruled out with a camera test, and that nothing is certain until then; acknowledges her fear.

Explains why an FOBT is not the right test: it is a screening test for people without symptoms; she has symptoms and visible bleeding, so a negative kit would not reassure and she needs a colonoscopy.
check.d: Credit whether explained in Part 1, when Jane asks, or in Part 2.

check.x: Arranges investigation of the bowel:

kids.x: Gives a structured ISBAR handover with a clear request for urgent colonoscopy (and gastroscopy), and refers urgently (not routine) to gastroenterology or colorectal surgery for colonoscopy with biopsy, with a referral letter that includes the symptoms, results, brother's diagnosis at 48 and penicillin allergy; phones the unit if needed.
kids.d: The critical element is an urgent (not routine) referral for colonoscopy. The letter contents and phoning the unit are not required for the critical mark.

kids.x: Asks for a gastroscopy at the same time and checks coeliac serology, because iron deficiency in a postmenopausal woman can also come from the upper gut.
kids.d: Optional extra credit: urinalysis for haematuria.

check.x: Starts oral iron replacement, warns that it can worsen constipation and turn stools dark, follows the endoscopy unit's instructions about stopping it before bowel preparation, and plans a repeat FBC to check the response.
check.d: Award for starting oral iron plus at least two of: constipation or dark stool warning, stopping before bowel preparation per unit instructions, repeat FBC. Accept a once-daily or alternate-day regimen, for example about 100–200 mg elemental iron once daily, or alternate days for better absorption and tolerability (eTG); IV iron if oral is not tolerated.

check.x: Offers macrogol rather than more fibre, fluids and activity, and smoking cessation support (brief advice, Quitline, pharmacotherapy).
Safety netting

Tells her to go to the ED or call 000 for heavy bleeding or clots, black tarry stools, feeling faint, breathless or chest pain, or severe tummy pain, vomiting, a swollen tummy, or not passing wind or stool; and to see the GP sooner if she loses weight, gets more tired, or her bowel habit or bleeding gets worse, or if she has not heard about her colonoscopy appointment within about a week.
check.d: Award for at least three red flags in plain words, linked to the ED or 000.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: a GP review after the colonoscopy to go through the results, and a repeat FBC on iron.
check.d: The critical element is a named plan to review the colonoscopy result. The repeat FBC alone does not earn the mark.

check.x: Checks her understanding and invites questions.

part2.lead: Jane had blood tests taken on the day you saw her, and she has come back two days later for the results. Here they are.
part2.patient:
Ask this question once while the candidate explains the plan:

  • "Do you think it's cancer, like my brother?"

You are anxious but you appreciate honesty. If the candidate falsely reassures you ("I'm sure it's nothing"), say: "But my brother was told that too." If the candidate uses jargon such as "colonoscopy", "iron deficiency" or "staging" without explaining it, ask what it means.

handover.label: Full blood count
handover.result: Collected at the first visit. Blood film: hypochromic, microcytic red cells with some pencil cells, consistent with iron deficiency. Mild thrombocytosis, likely reactive.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 108 is a mild anaemia. MCV 76 and MCH 24 are low and RDW 17.2 is high, so it is microcytic and hypochromic with varied red cell size; the film shows pencil cells. Platelets 418 are mildly raised; white cells are normal.
  • For Jane: this is the pattern of iron deficiency anaemia, and it explains her fatigue and pallor. The reactive thrombocytosis fits ongoing blood loss.
  • What it changes: together with blood mixed with the stool, it makes a bleeding colorectal lesion the leading concern and adds weight to an urgent colonoscopy. Needs iron studies to confirm (given) and a repeat FBC on treatment.

handover.label: Iron studies
handover.result: Collected at the first visit. Comment: iron studies consistent with iron deficiency.
handover.model:
• Read: ferritin 8 is low (below 30 confirms iron deficiency); serum iron 5 and transferrin saturation 5% are low, and transferrin 3.9 is high.
  • For Jane: absolute iron deficiency. She is postmenopausal, takes no NSAIDs and has no other obvious source, so this is blood loss from the gut until proven otherwise, and her visible blood points to the colon.
  • What it changes: iron deficiency anaemia in a postmenopausal woman needs a colonoscopy and a gastroscopy, plus coeliac serology. Start oral iron now, but do not let a response to iron delay the investigations.

handover.label: Biochemistry and thyroid function
handover.model:
• Read: sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine and eGFR normal. Corrected calcium 2.34 and albumin 40 normal. Bilirubin, ALT, ALP and GGT normal. TSH 1.6 normal.
  • For Jane: no hypothyroidism and no hypercalcaemia to explain the constipation (and no hypocalcaemia from her denosumab). Normal kidney function is a useful baseline before bowel preparation and any contrast CT. Normal liver tests are reassuring but do not exclude liver metastases.
  • What it changes: the reversible metabolic causes of constipation are excluded, which leaves a structural cause in the bowel as the main concern.

ask: You are now calling the gastroenterology registrar at the local hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Jane Doe, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Explain to Jane your management plan, here in general practice.
Before Jane leaves, tell her what to look out for and what follow-up you will arrange.
expect:
• Identify: self, intern at the practice; Jane Doe, 62.
  • Situation: change in bowel habit with rectal bleeding and iron deficiency anaemia; suspected colorectal cancer; requesting urgent colonoscopy.
  • Background: 5–6 months, daily to every 3–4 days, straining, tenesmus, blood mixed with stool, fatigue; no weight loss or obstruction. Brother CRC at 48. Smoker. Penicillin allergy.
  • Assessment: mild pallor, abdomen normal, PR no mass but dark red blood mixed with stool. Hb 108, MCV 76: microcytic anaemia; platelets 418, mildly raised, likely reactive; ferritin 8, TSAT 5%: iron deficiency. TSH, calcium, UEC and LFTs normal.
  • Recommendation: urgent colonoscopy, with gastroscopy for the iron deficiency; starting oral iron; please advise on timing.

Most likely: colorectal cancer until proven otherwise (probably left-sided or rectosigmoid). New change in bowel habit for months at 62, blood mixed with stool, tenesmus, iron deficiency anaemia, brother diagnosed at 48, smoker.

  • Recurrent haemorrhoids: for: previous haemorrhoidectomy, straining. Against: blood mixed in, not on the paper; none on PR; does not explain the change in habit or anaemia.
  • Diverticular disease: for: age, constipation. Against: diverticulosis is usually silent and does not cause a progressive change in habit or chronic iron deficiency; no LIF pain or fever to suggest diverticulitis; diverticular bleeding is usually sudden, painless and large.
  • Functional constipation or IBS-C: for: straining. Against: new at 62 with bleeding and anaemia; a diagnosis of exclusion.
  • Hypothyroidism or hypercalcaemia: for: constipation, fatigue. Against: normal TSH and corrected calcium.
  • Upper GI source of iron loss: why a gastroscopy is added.

1. Explain honestly in plain words: the symptoms and anaemia need a camera test to look for bowel cancer; nothing is certain yet.
  2. Not an FOBT: it is a screening test for people without symptoms; a negative kit would not rule anything out.
  3. Urgent referral to gastroenterology or colorectal surgery for colonoscopy with biopsy, plus gastroscopy and coeliac serology for the iron deficiency. Letter with symptoms, results, family history and penicillin allergy; phone if needed.
  4. Oral iron once daily or on alternate days; warn about constipation and dark stools; follow the unit's bowel preparation instructions.
  5. Symptoms: fluids, osmotic laxative (macrogol) rather than more fibre.
  6. Smoking cessation, exercise.

• Go to the ED or call 000 for heavy bleeding or clots, black tarry stools, feeling faint, breathless or chest pain, or severe tummy pain, vomiting, a swollen tummy or not passing wind or stool (a blocked bowel).
  • See the GP sooner for weight loss, worsening tiredness, or worse bleeding or bowel habit, or if no colonoscopy appointment arrives within about a week.
  • Follow-up: GP review after the colonoscopy to go through the results (with her husband if she wishes), repeat FBC on iron, and her future surveillance once the results are known.
  • Close: checks Jane understands the plan and invites her questions.

ddx.dx: Colorectal cancer (probably left-sided or rectosigmoid) with iron deficiency anaemia
ddx.for: Five to six months of new constipation at 62 with straining, tenesmus, blood mixed with the stool, fatigue, iron deficiency anaemia, a brother diagnosed at 48 and smoking.
ddx.against: No weight loss, abdominal pain or obstruction, and no mass on abdominal or rectal examination.
Blood is mixed through the stool rather than on the paper, there are no haemorrhoids on rectal examination or proctoscopy, and haemorrhoids do not explain the change in habit.

Diverticulosis is usually silent and does not cause a progressive change in habit or chronic iron deficiency; no LIF pain or fever to suggest diverticulitis; diverticular bleeding is usually sudden, painless and large.

ddx.dx: Functional constipation or constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome
ddx.for: Constipation with straining and a poor response to fibre.
ddx.against: New onset at 62 with no abdominal pain or bloating, and bleeding with iron deficiency anaemia, so it can only be diagnosed once structural disease is excluded.
No cold intolerance or weight gain, and a normal TSH.

ddx.dx: Upper gastrointestinal source of iron deficiency (gastric cancer, peptic ulcer, coeliac disease)
ddx.for: Iron deficiency anaemia in a postmenopausal woman, and she smokes.
ddx.against: No dyspepsia, weight loss or melaena, and the visible blood and change in bowel habit point to the colon.

guide:
This is a general practice station, so there is no observation chart: give the observations from the Exam findings when the candidate asks for them. In Part 1 the examiner gives findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. If the candidate asks for tests in Part 1, say the bloods have been taken and the results will come in Part 2. Jane asks once in Part 1 for "one of those poo test kits"; credit the FOBT explanation whether it is given then or in Part 2. In Part 2 hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order. Q1 is a simulated phone call to the registrar. For Q3 and Q4 the candidate speaks directly to Jane, who is present. Jane asks her question once during Q3.

A high-performing candidate characterises the bowel change and the bleeding, separates fresh blood from melaena, screens for red flags and obstruction, rules out the other causes, takes a careful family history (including other relatives, Lynch-type cancers and whether her brother had genetic or tumour testing), and performs a rectal examination with a chaperone. In Part 2 they recognise iron deficiency anaemia, treat colorectal cancer as the leading diagnosis without telling her she has it, explain clearly why an FOBT is the wrong test, refer urgently for colonoscopy (with gastroscopy for the iron deficiency), start iron, and give specific red flags and follow-up.

A borderline candidate takes a generic constipation history, does not quantify the bleeding or ask about melaena, omits the rectal examination, or blames the haemorrhoids. They may give her the FOBT kit, refer routinely, increase her fibre and review in three months, or falsely reassure her.
explain:
Diagnosis

Jane most likely has colorectal cancer until proven otherwise. She has a new and persistent change in bowel habit at 62, straining and tenesmus, small amounts of blood mixed with the stool, and fatigue. Her blood tests show iron deficiency anaemia, and her brother was diagnosed at 48. Smoking adds to the risk. A tumour in the left colon or rectosigmoid would fit best: left-sided cancers narrow the bowel and change the bowel habit, and they bleed visibly. Tenesmus suggests a lesion low in the bowel. A normal rectal examination does not exclude this, because most of the colon is out of reach of the finger.

Colorectal cancer as the red-flag diagnosis in constipation

Colorectal cancer should be considered in every constipation history. Risk factors include age, a family history, hereditary syndromes (familial adenomatous polyposis, Lynch syndrome), inflammatory bowel disease, smoking, alcohol, obesity, low physical activity and a diet high in red and processed meat. Cancer is often silent. When it does cause symptoms, they include a change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, abdominal pain, constitutional symptoms or anaemia. Right-sided tumours tend to be insidious and present with iron deficiency anaemia. Left-sided tumours tend to obstruct and change the bowel habit. A benign cause such as haemorrhoids does not exclude cancer. Jane's previous haemorrhoids are a trap: blood mixed through the stool, a change in habit and anaemia are not explained by haemorrhoids.

Differentials that matter

  • Haemorrhoids and anal fissure: bright red blood on the paper or in the bowl, with a fissure causing pain on defecation. Jane has neither on examination.
  • Diverticular disease: common at her age. Diverticulitis causes left iliac fossa pain and fever, and diverticular bleeding is usually sudden, painless and large.
  • Functional constipation or IBS-C: diagnosed only after red flags have been dealt with. A new onset after 50 is itself a red flag.
  • Inflammatory bowel disease: causes blood and mucus with diarrhoea and urgency rather than constipation.
  • Metabolic and drug causes: hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, and constipating medicines (opioids, iron, calcium, anticholinergics). These are excluded by her history and bloods.
  • Obstruction: she is still passing wind and has no vomiting or distension. A stenosing tumour can progress to obstruction, which is why it is a safety-netting point.
  • Neurological and pelvic causes: cauda equina symptoms, urinary retention, and PV bleeding from a gynaecological cancer.

Interpreting the results

  • Full blood count: a microcytic, hypochromic anaemia (Hb 108, MCV 76) with a high RDW, pencil cells and a reactive thrombocytosis is typical of iron deficiency from chronic blood loss.
  • Iron studies: a ferritin of 8 confirms iron deficiency. Low iron and transferrin saturation and a high transferrin support it.
  • Biochemistry: a normal TSH and calcium exclude hypothyroidism and hypercalcaemia. Normal liver tests do not exclude metastases.

In a man or a postmenopausal woman, iron deficiency anaemia has a gastrointestinal cause (blood loss or malabsorption) until proven otherwise. GESA advises colonoscopy and gastroscopy (bidirectional endoscopy) together with coeliac serology and urinalysis for haematuria.

Why not an FOBT

The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program sends a free immunochemical FOBT every two years to people aged 50 to 74, and people aged 45 to 49 can ask for one. It is a screening test for people without symptoms. Jane has symptoms, visible bleeding and anaemia, so she needs a diagnostic colonoscopy. A negative FOBT would falsely reassure her and delay the diagnosis. Separately, a first-degree relative diagnosed before 55 puts her above average risk. Under the Cancer Council Australia guidelines this calls for colonoscopic surveillance rather than FOBT screening alone. Her future surveillance interval will depend on what her colonoscopy shows and on her family history.

Management

  • Urgent referral to gastroenterology or colorectal surgery for colonoscopy with biopsy, the gold-standard test. Add a gastroscopy for the iron deficiency. The Optimal Care Pathway for colorectal cancer expects people with symptoms of concern to be referred and investigated promptly, within weeks, not months. The referral should state the red flags, the results, the family history and her allergy.
  • Iron replacement: oral iron, for example about 100–200 mg elemental iron once daily, or alternate days for better absorption and tolerability (eTG). Warn her that it can worsen constipation and darken the stools. Use IV iron if oral iron is not tolerated or does not work. A good response to iron does not remove the need for endoscopy.
  • Constipation: eTG advises fluids and activity. When fibre fails, an osmotic laxative such as macrogol is the next step. Avoid adding more bulking agent while a narrowing lesion is possible. Check her calcium and vitamin D intake on denosumab; calcium supplements also constipate.
  • If cancer is confirmed: staging with CEA and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis (MRI of the pelvis for rectal cancer; PET in selected cases). Management is through a multidisciplinary team. Colon cancer is treated with surgical resection with the regional lymph nodes, plus adjuvant chemotherapy depending on stage. Rectal cancer may need chemoradiotherapy as well; radiotherapy is not usually used for colon cancer. CEA is a staging and monitoring marker, not a diagnostic test.
  • Family: a diagnosis at 48 raises the question of Lynch syndrome. Ask whether her brother's tumour was tested for mismatch repair deficiency, and refer to a familial cancer clinic if the family meets the criteria.
  • Risk factors: smoking cessation support and regular physical activity.

Safety netting and follow-up

She should go to the ED or call 000 for heavy rectal bleeding, black tarry stools, feeling faint or breathless, chest pain, or symptoms of a blocked bowel (severe pain, vomiting, a swollen tummy, not passing wind or stool). She should see the GP sooner if she loses weight, gets more tired, her symptoms worsen, or no appointment arrives. Book a GP review after the colonoscopy to go through the results, with a repeat FBC on iron.
points: A new, persistent change in bowel habit at an older age, especially with rectal bleeding, tenesmus or anaemia, is colorectal cancer until proven otherwise, even when there is a benign explanation such as previous haemorrhoids.

Distinguish fresh blood (on the paper, in the bowl or mixed with the stool) from melaena, and always perform a rectal examination with a chaperone; a normal rectal examination does not exclude a higher lesion.

Iron deficiency anaemia in a man or a postmenopausal woman has a gastrointestinal cause (blood loss or malabsorption) until proven otherwise and calls for colonoscopy and gastroscopy plus coeliac serology.
An FOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms; a symptomatic patient needs an urgent diagnostic colonoscopy, and a negative FOBT would falsely reassure.

A first-degree relative with colorectal cancer diagnosed before 55 puts a person above average risk and raises the question of Lynch syndrome; ask about the wider family and the relative's tumour testing.

Colorectal cancer is staged with CEA and CT (MRI of the pelvis for rectal cancer) and treated through a multidisciplinary team: resection with regional lymph nodes ± adjuvant chemotherapy, with chemoradiotherapy for rectal cancer.
